name: CW (Morse Code)
frequency_area: Lower portion of most amateur HF bands (e.g. 3.5-3.6, 7.0-7.1, 14.0-14.1 MHz)
modulation: On/off keying of a continuous carrier
identifying_characteristics: A single steady tone switching on and off in short (dit) and long (dah) bursts - unmistakable once heard. Often sounds musical/rhythmic from a skilled operator. See the Morse Code Reference guide above for the actual code table.

name: SSB Voice (Single Sideband)
frequency_area: Most amateur HF voice sub-bands, marine HF, some utility/military HF
modulation: SSB (USB above 10 MHz by convention, LSB below, on amateur bands)
identifying_characteristics: If tuned slightly off-frequency, voice sounds high-pitched, garbled, or 'Donald Duck'-like - this is the single most reliable SSB identifier. Correctly tuned, it sounds like natural (if slightly narrow/nasal) voice. No squelch 'quieting' the way FM has - background noise is continuous.

name: AM Voice / Broadcast
frequency_area: AM broadcast band (0.53-1.7 MHz), airband (108-137 MHz), some shortwave broadcast
identifying_characteristics: Full, natural-sounding voice/music with no 'quieting' effect - background static fades in/out smoothly rather than snapping open/closed like FM squelch. On airband specifically: short, clipped transmissions, standard phraseology, frequent callsigns/tail numbers.

name: NFM Voice (Narrowband FM)
frequency_area: Most VHF/UHF voice services: amateur 2m/70cm, marine VHF, GMRS/FRS/MURS, public safety
identifying_characteristics: Clean, quiet audio when a signal is present; squelch snaps fully open/closed rather than fading gradually the way AM/SSB static does. Weak signals often 'pop' or distort rather than just getting quieter. The most common voice mode a wideband receiver will encounter overall.

name: NOAA SAME / EAS Digital Alert Burst
modulation: AFSK (audio frequency-shift keying) digital burst, on an NFM carrier
identifying_characteristics: A distinctive harsh, buzzing warble lasting a few seconds, immediately before a spoken weather alert - this is the Specific Area Message Encoding (SAME) header that tells weather radios which counties to alert for. Unmistakable once heard once; often followed by two loud attention tones, then the spoken message.

name: DTMF (Touch-Tone)
frequency_area: Anywhere voice services are used - repeater access codes, phone patches
modulation: Dual-tone multi-frequency (two simultaneous audio tones per digit)
identifying_characteristics: The familiar telephone keypad tones - a short burst of one or more distinct two-tone beeps. On amateur/business radio, usually heard briefly at the start of a transmission (repeater control/access) rather than as a sustained signal.

name: RTTY (Radioteletype)
frequency_area: Amateur HF digital sub-bands, some utility/military HF
identifying_characteristics: A steady two-tone warbling/trilling sound at a constant rhythm - distinctly more mechanical and continuous than CW's dit-dah pattern. Sounds a little like an old dot-matrix printer or a rapid two-note siren.

name: Packet / APRS Burst
frequency_area: 144.390 MHz (APRS, North America); various amateur packet frequencies
modulation: AFSK (1200 baud typical) on an NFM carrier
identifying_characteristics: A brief (roughly 1 second), harsh, buzzing burst - often described as sounding like a short 'brrrt' or a modem handshake fragment. Position/status data (APRS) or general packet traffic, not voice - if you hear this on 144.390 MHz in the US, it's very likely APRS.
